summary: Second batch: 40 MORE quotes on being ready, from different source pools than batch 1

lines.line: Young or old, we think the big changes are behind us. They are not.
Every body has hard days. The wise expect them, and stay calm.
A climber called Grandma Whitney took up jogging. Why? It made climbing much easier.
So pack before you go. Out for a day? Take bread for a week.
First in the bag, a strong body. The mind cannot carry the load alone.
Next, a breath habit: slow, deep and steady, until the mind finds balance.
And a mind like a mirror: it meets everything and holds on to nothing.
But stored bread is not eaten bread. Only what you practise becomes you.
So practise every day. Busy? Do one asana. But never skip completely.
Your daily bread: Ashtanga. Asana for strength, breath for lightness, turning inward for calm.
Every day brings hidden gifts. Leave them unused, and it quietly takes them back.
We want to know what's inside. But it's all uncertain. So, be patient.
Patient, not idle: young Iyengar began yoga to grow strong for life's challenges.
The body needs a little work each day, never too tiring, never forced.
And after 40, a more flexible body went with more flexible blood vessels.
Not proud in success, not crushed in defeat. Whatever comes, never lose heart.
At 14, Midori's string snapped on stage, then another. Calmly, she finished the piece.
Musicians say: skip practice one day, you notice. Skip three, everyone notices.
And years of steady yoga, it is said, build an unshakable mind.
Shaping each day is the highest art. Open tomorrow's gifts on your Ashtanga mat.
Even Kipchoge tested his shoes in Kenya, and still had a bad race day.
Yet a Zen master said: every day is a good day. Even that one.
So in Thailand we say: going into the forest? Don't forget your bush knife.
Sharpen daily: one small hard thing, so the day of need finds you trained.
What does yoga give first? Lightness, health, steadiness, a bright face, a clear voice.
Fitness went with a steadier heart under stress, and a faster return to calm.
When trouble comes, smile with a patient, hopeful heart. Nothing has more power.
Sax player Sonny Rollins practised for hours every day. Cold? He played in gloves.
The nose-tip gaze, an Ashtanga drishti, kept up for months, steadies a wandering mind.
Karate isn't only in the dojo. Your morning Ashtanga goes with you all day.
The alarm rings. What will today bring? Nobody knows. So start living now.
And live ready: the wise look ahead, so trouble cannot shake them.
How? Dancer Twyla Tharp's ritual wasn't the workout. It was getting into the taxi.
Two short, heavy lifting sessions a week went with stronger bones in older women.
Eat just enough, keep regular hours, never overdo it: body and spirit stay together.
Relaxed face, calm full breath, soft muscles: where could tomorrow's worries get in?
Ayurveda's alarm clock: a healthy person rises before dawn, to protect a long life.
Then the same asanas daily: what felt impossible on Monday is normal by Saturday.
With morning yoga, Sting said, he had more energy, got more done, felt calmer.
So set the alarm: Ashtanga each morning eases stiffness, and your work goes better.

final.checks:
BASE AND GRAFTS: I used Draft A as the base because it was cleaner on the rules and had the stronger hooks (R2, Kipchoge, the alarm). I then made the changes below.

C1 renamed "Bread for a Week": the bread runs through three slides. Slide 4 packs bread for a week. Slide 8 says stored bread is not eaten bread. Slide 10 makes Ashtanga "your daily bread". T4 now comes before J3, so the bag appears right before "First in the bag". Slide 10 (I12) now says "turning inward for calm" (pratyahara) instead of the vague "inward calm".

C2 rebuilt as "The Day's Hidden Gifts":
- E1 is reworded as a stronger hook: unused gifts are taken back.
- T2 (Grete Waitz) is swapped for J2 (Ajahn Chah, a Thai monk). Its quote has no payoff: it never says she finished or won, so the slide left readers hanging.
- R11 (rod in a tilted frame, too abstract for a stranger) is swapped for E11 (William James: years of yoga build an unshakable mind).
- I10 is swapped for T9 (the musicians' saying). It follows Midori's story, so the music thread carries on.
- Slide 10 links back to slide 1: "Open tomorrow's gifts on your Ashtanga mat."

C3: R8 (mindfulness and the amygdala) is swapped for R7 (fit hearts stay steadier under stress). R7 makes the step from body to mind, and it is easier to follow. Slide 10 now links back to the tool: "Your morning Ashtanga goes with you all day."

C4:
- I2 now says "And live ready", so it no longer clashes with Seneca's "live now".
- R5 now comes before J6. Tharp's gym leads into lifting, and then "never overdo it" balances it.
- J6 now keeps the quote's own result: "body and spirit stay together".
- I11 is framed as "Ayurveda's alarm clock".

RULE CHECKS (run by script):
- 40 lines, 40 different ids, none repeated.
- Every line is 14 words or fewer, with no long or en dash.
- The words pose, war, accident, flood, storm, rain, water and cause do not appear.
- Every slide 10 names Ashtanga.
- No author appears twice in one carousel. William James (E3, E8, E11) and Tiruvalluvar (I1, I2, I8) each appear in three different carousels.
- Each carousel has all six lanes: yoga or Indian text, lineage teacher, Asian or Russian proverb, Western writer, true story and science.
- Arc order is right in every carousel. Stage totals: unknown_day 7, prepare_before 7, body_ready 6, mind_ready 7, daily_practice 6, ashtanga_tool 7.
- Science lines R6, R7 and R5 say "went with". R2 only reports what people expected, so it makes no causal claim.

UNUSED IDS: I3, I4, I6, I7, I10, L1, L2, L4, L5, L6, L7, J8, J9, J10, J12, E4, E5, E7, E9, T2, T5, T6, T8, T11, R1, R3, R4, R8, R9, R10, R11, R12. T8 (Lynn Hill's slip) and I3 were left out to stay clear of accident images.

FOR BOONCHU TO CONFIRM:
- Four lines apply a general yoga or training quote to Ashtanga by analogy. The credit still shows the real source.
  - I12: Gheranda's "pranayama" is rendered as "breath", and mudra is left out.
  - L11: the quote's "nasal gaze" is called an Ashtanga drishti.
  - L12: Iyengar's "regular morning practice" becomes "Ashtanga each morning".
  - J11: Funakoshi's karate saying.
- T12 says only "yoga", because Sting's quote does not say Ashtanga.
- J4 is in Boonchu's voice ("So in Thailand we say").
- I1 writes "Every body" as two words on purpose (the body is sorrow's target), so it is not a typo for "everybody".
- T4 gives no age for Hulda Crooks, because the quote does not say when she started jogging.
- R5 says "older women". The study was in postmenopausal women with low bone mass, about 65 on average.
- T7 says "then another": the second string broke on a borrowed violin.

rows.line: Young or old, we think the big changes are behind us. They are not.
rows.who: Jordi Quoidbach, Daniel T. Gilbert and Timothy D. Wilson (Harvard University and University of Virginia; PubMed lists Quoidbach under the National Fund for Scientific Research, Brussels)
rows.quote: Young people, middle-aged people, and older people all believed they had changed a lot in the past but would change relatively little in the future.
rows.source: Quoidbach J, Gilbert DT, Wilson TD. The end of history illusion. Science 2013;339(6115):96-98. PMID 23288539. doi:10.1126/science.1229294

rows.line: Every body has hard days. The wise expect them, and stay calm.
rows.credit: Tiruvalluvar · Tirukkural 627, tr. G. U. Pope
rows.who: Tiruvalluvar
rows.quote: 'Man's frame is sorrow's target', the noble mind reflects, / Nor meets with troubled mind the sorrows it expects.
rows.source: Tirukkural 627 (ch. 63, 'Hopefulness in Trouble'), verse translation by G. U. Pope, The 'Sacred' Kurral, London: W. H. Allen, 1886 (Project Madurai e-text, p. 126)

rows.line: A climber called Grandma Whitney took up jogging. Why? It made climbing much easier.
rows.who: Hulda Crooks, mountain climber ('Grandma Whitney'), USA
rows.quote: it made climbing so much easier
rows.source: Myrna Oliver, Los Angeles Times, 26 Nov 1997, reprinted in The Seattle Times archive

rows.line: So pack before you go. Out for a day? Take bread for a week.
rows.who: Russian proverb
rows.quote: Going for a day? Take bread for a week.
rows.source: V. I. Dal, Poslovitsy russkogo naroda (Proverbs of the Russian People), 1862, section 'Запас' (Provision); literal translation

rows.line: First in the bag, a strong body. The mind cannot carry the load alone.
rows.credit: Montaigne · Of the Education of Children
rows.who: Michel de Montaigne, French essayist (1533-1592)
rows.quote: It is not enough to fortify his soul; you are also to make his sinews strong; for the soul will be oppressed if not assisted by the members, and would have too hard a task to discharge two offices alone.
rows.source: Essays I.25 "Of the Education of Children" (I.26 in modern numbering), tr. Charles Cotton (1685-86), ed. W. Carew Hazlitt (1877); Project Gutenberg #3600

rows.line: Next, a breath habit: slow, deep and steady, until the mind finds balance.
rows.who: Shri Yogendra, founder of The Yoga Institute (India and America)
rows.quote: ...the habit of deep, prolonged, rhythmic breathing, in due course, establishes a corresponding state of mental equipoise.
rows.source: Shri Yogendra, Hatha Yoga Simplified (Bombay: The Yoga Institute; first edition April 1931), ch. I 'Care of the Respiratory Apparatus', section 'Sedative Nervous Effects', p. 51 of the archive.org scan (a reprint from 1950 or later)

rows.line: And a mind like a mirror: it meets everything and holds on to nothing.
rows.credit: Zhuangzi · ch. 7, tr. H. A. Giles, 1889
rows.who: Zhuangzi, Daoist sage
rows.quote: The perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing: it refuses nothing. It receives, but does not keep.
rows.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 7, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer (London: Bernard Quaritch, 1889)

rows.line: But stored bread is not eaten bread. Only what you practise becomes you.
rows.who: Epictetus, Greek Stoic teacher (1st-2nd century AD)
rows.quote: ...it is one thing to lay up bread and wine as in a storehouse, and another thing to eat. That which has been eaten, is digested, distributed, and is become sinews, flesh, bones, blood, healthy color, healthy breath.
rows.source: Discourses II.9 ("That when we cannot fulfil that which the character of a man promises, we assume the character of a philosopher"), tr. George Long (1877); Project Gutenberg #10661 (A Selection from the Discourses)

rows.line: So practise every day. Busy? Do one asana. But never skip completely.
rows.who: Indra Devi, yoga teacher
rows.quote: But the most important thing is to do them regularly, without skipping. If you happen not to have time for all of them, do just a few, perhaps even only one when you are in a great hurry—but never omit them entirely.
rows.source: Indra Devi, Yoga for You: A Complete 6 Weeks' Course for Home Practice (Preston: A. Thomas & Co., 1960), Lesson One, First Week, 'What the Course Is and How to Use It'

rows.line: Your daily bread: Ashtanga. Asana for strength, breath for lightness, turning inward for calm.
rows.credit: Gheranda Samhita 1.10-11 · tr. S. C. Vasu
rows.who: Gheranda, teaching Chanda Kapali, in the Gheranda Samhita
rows.quote: Asana or posture gives Driddhata or strength; Mudra gives Sthirata or steadiness; Pratyahara gives Dhairyata or calmness; Pranayama gives lightness or Laghima ...
rows.source: Gheranda Samhita 1.10-11, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu, The Gheranda Samhita, first published 1914-15 (Sri Satguru reprint 1979)

rows.line: Every day brings hidden gifts. Leave them unused, and it quietly takes them back.
rows.credit: Ralph Waldo Emerson · Works and Days, 1870
rows.who: Ralph Waldo Emerson, American essayist (1803-1882)
rows.quote: [The days] come and go like muffled and veiled figures, sent from a distant friendly party; but they say nothing; and if we do not use the gifts they bring, they carry them as silently away.
rows.source: "Works and Days", in Society and Solitude: Twelve Chapters (Boston: Fields, Osgood & Co., 1870), essay begins p. 139; Project Gutenberg eBook #69258

rows.line: We want to know what's inside. But it's all uncertain. So, be patient.
rows.credit: Ajahn Chah · Not Sure!, Dhamma talk
rows.who: Ajahn Chah, Thai forest monk (Wat Nong Pah Pong)
rows.quote: In truth it's all uncertain, but our desires want things to be certain. What can we do? We must be patient.
rows.source: Ajahn Chah, '"Not Sure!" - The Standard of the Noble Ones', informal evening talk to monks and novices at his kuti (footnote 1 dates it 1980; footnote 8 dates 'this year' to 2522 BE = 1979 CE). In The Teachings of Ajahn Chah on ajahnchah.org (listed in the 'Food for the Heart' part), © Wat Nong Pah Pong 2007; translator not named

rows.line: Patient, not idle: young Iyengar began yoga to grow strong for life's challenges.
rows.credit: B. K. S. Iyengar · Light on Life, 2005
rows.who: B. K. S. Iyengar, yoga teacher, recalling how he began yoga as a teenager
rows.quote: ...my brother-in-law recommended a stiff regime of yoga practice to knock me into shape and strengthen me up to face life's trials and challenges as I approached adulthood.
rows.source: B. K. S. Iyengar, Light on Life (Rodale, 2005), as quoted by NPR: Allison Aubrey, ''Light on Life': B.K.S. Iyengar's Yoga Insights', Morning Edition, 10 November 2005 (quotes credited 'courtesy of Rodale, Inc.'); chapter not confirmed

rows.line: The body needs a little work each day, never too tiring, never forced.
rows.who: A 'Perfected One' (真人, zhenren) quoted by the Tang physician Sun Simiao
rows.quote: The way to nourish life: always do a little work, but never to great fatigue, and never force what you cannot bear.
rows.source: Sun Simiao, Beiji Qianjin Yaofang (Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold), c. 652, 'Nourishing Life' (養性), section 道林養性第二; juan 81 in the Siku Quanshu text on Wikisource (juan numbers differ between editions); literal translation

rows.line: And after 40, a more flexible body went with more flexible blood vessels.
rows.credit: Yamamoto et al. · Am J Physiol, 2009
rows.who: Kenta Yamamoto, Motohiko Miyachi et al., National Institute of Health and Nutrition, Tokyo
rows.quote: These findings suggest that flexibility may be a predictor of arterial stiffening, independent of other components of fitness.
rows.source: Yamamoto K, Kawano H, Gando Y, et al. Poor trunk flexibility is associated with arterial stiffening. American Journal of Physiology: Heart and Circulatory Physiology 2009;297(4):H1314-H1318. PMID 19666849. doi:10.1152/ajpheart.00061.2009

rows.line: Not proud in success, not crushed in defeat. Whatever comes, never lose heart.
rows.who: Charaka Samhita (rules of right conduct taught by Atreya)
rows.quote: Do not give way to anger and joy; do not nurse your sorrows; be not arrogant in success and dejected in defeat; ... do not grow complacent with your achievements; do not lose heart.
rows.source: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 8.27 (ch. 8, 'The Discipline of the Senses'), tr. Shree Gulabkunverba Ayurvedic Society, Jamnagar, 1949 (wisdomlib transcription; its typo 'iu' corrected to 'in')

rows.line: At 14, Midori's string snapped on stage, then another. Calmly, she finished the piece.
rows.who: Midori (Midori Goto), violinist, aged 14, at Tanglewood, 1986
rows.quote: During the fifth and final movement, the highest string on Midori's smaller-than-normal violin snapped. Unfazed, she borrowed concertmaster Malcolm Lowe's instrument, and when the same string on that violin also broke, she finished the performance on the violin of assistant concertmaster Max Hobart.
rows.source: A. Z. Madonna, 'Seiji Ozawa's legacy shines on stage at Symphony Hall', Boston Globe, 7 Nov 2025. Confirmed by Midori's own site: 'In 1986, at the age of 14, Midori performed the Serenade with the Boston Symphony Orchestra at Tanglewood... She never missed a note.'

rows.line: Musicians say: skip practice one day, you notice. Skip three, everyone notices.
rows.who: Musicians' saying, earliest known attribution to pianist Hans von Bülow (1877)
rows.quote: If I stop practice for one day, I notice it in my playing; if I stop two days, my friends notice it; if I stop three days, the public notices it.
rows.source: Boston Evening Transcript, 'Musical Matters', 3 Sep 1877, p. 6, col. 2, as traced by Quote Investigator, 'If I Don't Practice for One Day, I Know It...', 8 Dec 2024

rows.line: And years of steady yoga, it is said, build an unshakable mind.
rows.credit: William James · The Energies of Men, 1907
rows.who: William James, American psychologist and philosopher (1842-1910)
rows.quote: ...by Hatha Yoga, Raja Yoga, Karma Yoga, or whatever code of practice it might be, Hindu aspirants to perfection have trained themselves, month in and out, for years. The result claimed... is strength of character, personal power, unshakability of soul.
rows.source: "The Energies of Men" (presidential address, American Philosophical Association, Columbia University, 28 Dec 1906; Philosophical Review, Jan 1907); popular version (American Magazine, Oct 1907) reprinted in Memories and Studies (Longmans, Green, 1911); Project Gutenberg #20768

rows.line: Shaping each day is the highest art. Open tomorrow's gifts on your Ashtanga mat.
rows.who: Henry David Thoreau, American essayist (1817-1862)
rows.quote: I know of no more encouraging fact than the unquestionable ability of man to elevate his life by a conscious endeavor... To affect the quality of the day, that is the highest of arts.
rows.source: Walden (1854), ch. 2 "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"; Project Gutenberg #205

rows.line: Even Kipchoge tested his shoes in Kenya, and still had a bad race day.
rows.who: Eliud Kipchoge, marathon runner, Kenya
rows.quote: It wasn't a good day for me in these shoes, although they're actually very good. I tested them in Kenya, but just had bad luck on the day.
rows.source: After winning the Berlin Marathon, 27 Sep 2015. Quote from the Wall Street Journal, reprinted in Capital FM Kenya (Mutwiri Mutuota, 'Majors glory beckons for Berlin King Eliud', 28 Sep 2015). Race facts: Sports Illustrated (Chris Chavez), 27 Sep 2015.

rows.line: Yet a Zen master said: every day is a good day. Even that one.
rows.who: Yunmen Wenyan (864-949), Chan (Zen) master, China
rows.quote: Every day is a good day.
rows.source: Blue Cliff Record (Biyan lu), case 6 (碧巖錄第六則), compiled by Yuanwu Keqin, 1125; Chinese text on Wikisource 碧巖錄/卷第一; literal translation. Dictionary: Digital Daijisen and Koji Seigo o Shiru Jiten on Kotobank (日日是好日)

rows.line: So in Thailand we say: going into the forest? Don't forget your bush knife.
rows.credit: Thai saying · khao thuean ya luem phra
rows.who: Thai saying (สำนวน)
rows.quote: Going into the forest? Don't forget your bush knife.
rows.source: Thai saying. The Royal Institute (ORST) dictionary uses it as the example under เถื่อน ('น. ป่า เช่น เข้าเถื่อนอย่าลืมพร้า'; seen in a reproduction at online-english-thai-dictionary.com, because the ORST site was down). Meaning from Thai PBS Podcast, นิทานสุภาษิต EP. 34 'เข้าเถื่อนอย่าลืมพร้า เข้าป่าอย่าลืมมีด': 'ให้มีความรอบคอบ อย่าประมาท' (be careful, not careless), like carrying a knife into the forest for when it is needed. Also Thai Wiktionary and Wongnai. Literal translation

rows.line: Sharpen daily: one small hard thing, so the day of need finds you trained.
rows.who: William James, American psychologist and philosopher (1842-1910)
rows.quote: Keep the faculty of effort alive in you by a little gratuitous exercise every day... so that when the hour of dire need draws nigh, it may find you not unnerved and untrained to stand the test.
rows.source: The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. 4 "Habit", p. 126 (Classics in the History of Psychology e-text, York University)

rows.line: What does yoga give first? Lightness, health, steadiness, a bright face, a clear voice.
rows.who: Svetasvatara Upanishad
rows.quote: The first results of Yoga they call lightness, healthiness, steadiness, a good complexion, an easy pronunciation ...
rows.source: Svetasvatara Upanishad II.13, tr. F. Max Müller, The Upanishads Part II, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15, Oxford, 1884, p. 242

rows.line: Fitness went with a steadier heart under stress, and a faster return to calm.
rows.who: Kathleen Forcier, Laura R. Stroud et al., Centers for Behavioral and Preventive Medicine, Brown Medical School
rows.quote: ...fit individuals showed significantly attenuated heart rate and systolic blood pressure reactivity... Fit individuals also showed faster heart rate recovery...
rows.source: Forcier K, Stroud LR, Papandonatos GD, et al. Links between physical fitness and cardiovascular reactivity and recovery to psychological stressors: A meta-analysis. Health Psychology 2006;25(6):723-739. PMID 17100501. doi:10.1037/0278-6133.25.6.723

rows.line: When trouble comes, smile with a patient, hopeful heart. Nothing has more power.
rows.credit: Tiruvalluvar · Tirukkural 621, tr. G. U. Pope
rows.who: Tiruvalluvar
rows.quote: Smile, with patient, hopeful heart, in troublous hour; / Meet and so vanquish grief; nothing hath equal power.
rows.source: Tirukkural 621 (ch. 63, 'Hopefulness in Trouble'), verse translation by G. U. Pope, The 'Sacred' Kurral, London: W. H. Allen, 1886 (Project Madurai e-text, pp. 124-125)

rows.line: Sax player Sonny Rollins practised for hours every day. Cold? He played in gloves.
rows.who: Sonny Rollins, jazz saxophonist, USA
rows.quote: Well, I would play for a long time every day, often 14 or 15 hours. ... If it was cold, I'd play with gloves on; that was not a problem.
rows.source: John Fordham, ''I was so close to the sky. It was spiritual': Sonny Rollins on jazz landmark The Bridge at 60', The Guardian, 21 Jan 2022 (republished on Portside, 29 Jan 2022)

rows.line: The nose-tip gaze, an Ashtanga drishti, kept up for months, steadies a wandering mind.
rows.who: Swami Kuvalayananda, yoga teacher and researcher, founder of Kaivalyadhama, Lonavla
rows.quote: The Nasal Gaze is a fine exercise for the wandering mind. Its practice if undertaken with zest and carried over a period of some months continuously, has a perceptibly beneficial effect upon the unsteady mind.
rows.source: Swami Kuvalayananda, Popular Yoga: Asanas, Part One (Lonavla: Kaivalyadhama; Bombay, 1933), ch. III 'Meditative Poses', 'Nasagra-Drishti or the Nasal Gaze', p. 48

rows.line: Karate isn't only in the dojo. Your morning Ashtanga goes with you all day.
rows.who: Gichin Funakoshi, founder of Shotokan karate
rows.quote: Do not think karate is only in the dojo.
rows.source: Shōtōkan Nijū Kun (Twenty Precepts of Karate), no. 8, by Gichin Funakoshi. Said to have been written down around 1890; first published in Nakasone Genwa, Karate-dō Taikan (空手道大觀), 3 May 1938, frontispiece (per Japanese and English Wikipedia); literal translation

rows.line: The alarm rings. What will today bring? Nobody knows. So start living now.
rows.credit: Seneca · On the Shortness of Life 9.1
rows.who: Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher (1st century AD)
rows.quote: All things that are still to come lie in uncertainty; live straightway!
rows.source: On the Shortness of Life (De Brevitate Vitae) 9.1, tr. John W. Basore, Moral Essays vol. II, Loeb Classical Library, 1932 (Wikisource transcription)

rows.line: And live ready: the wise look ahead, so trouble cannot shake them.
rows.credit: Tiruvalluvar · Tirukkural 429, tr. G. U. Pope
rows.who: Tiruvalluvar
rows.quote: The wise with watchful soul who coming ills foresee; / From coming evil's dreaded shock are free.
rows.source: Tirukkural 429 (ch. 43, 'The Possession of Knowledge'), verse translation by G. U. Pope, The 'Sacred' Kurral, London: W. H. Allen, 1886 (Project Madurai e-text, p. 87)

rows.line: How? Dancer Twyla Tharp's ritual wasn't the workout. It was getting into the taxi.
rows.who: Twyla Tharp, dancer and choreographer, USA
rows.quote: The ritual is not the stretching and weight training I put my body through each morning at the gym; the ritual is the cab. The moment I tell the driver where to go I have completed the ritual.
rows.source: Twyla Tharp (with Mark Reiter), The Creative Habit: Learn It and Use It for Life, Simon & Schuster, 2003, ch. 2 'Rituals of Preparation'. Passage quoted on jamesclear.com.

rows.line: Two short, heavy lifting sessions a week went with stronger bones in older women.
rows.who: Steven L. Watson, Belinda R. Beck et al., Griffith University and Menzies Health Institute Queensland, Gold Coast, Australia (LIFTMOR trial)
rows.quote: Our novel, brief HiRIT [high-intensity resistance and impact training] program enhances indices of bone strength and functional performance in postmenopausal women with low bone mass.
rows.source: Watson SL, Weeks BK, Weis LJ, Harding AT, Horan SA, Beck BR. High-Intensity Resistance and Impact Training Improves Bone Mineral Density and Physical Function in Postmenopausal Women With Osteopenia and Osteoporosis: The LIFTMOR Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research 2018;33(2):211-220. PMID 28975661. doi:10.1002/jbmr.3284 (erratum JBMR 2019;34(3):572 corrects only Table 1 typos)

rows.line: Eat just enough, keep regular hours, never overdo it: body and spirit stay together.
rows.who: Qi Bo, physician-teacher in the Suwen
rows.quote: Those of old who knew the Way... ate and drank in measure, kept regular hours, and did not wear themselves out recklessly; so body and spirit stayed together.
rows.source: Suwen (Basic Questions), Chinese medical classic, ch. 1 'Shanggu tianzhen lun' (上古天真論); literal translation

rows.line: Relaxed face, calm full breath, soft muscles: where could tomorrow's worries get in?
rows.credit: William James · The Gospel of Relaxation
rows.who: William James, American psychologist and philosopher (1842-1910)
rows.quote: ...how can [the future and its worries] gain admission to your mind if your brow be unruffled, your respiration calm and complete, and your muscles all relaxed?
rows.source: "The Gospel of Relaxation", in Talks to Teachers on Psychology: and to Students on Some of Life's Ideals (New York: Henry Holt, 1899); Project Gutenberg #16287

rows.line: Ayurveda's alarm clock: a healthy person rises before dawn, to protect a long life.
rows.who: Vagbhata
rows.quote: A healthy person should rise at brahma muhurta, to protect their lifespan.
rows.source: Vagbhata, Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2.1 (Dinacharya, 'Daily Regimen' chapter), c. 600 CE (date debated); tr. from Sanskrit (literal rendering of the half-verse); Sanskrit as given by Dr J. V. Hebbar, easyayurveda.com

rows.line: Then the same asanas daily: what felt impossible on Monday is normal by Saturday.
rows.who: Indra Devi, yoga teacher
rows.quote: As you practice the same postures day by day, you will find your muscles stretching, your body growing more responsive and better controlled, until what seemed unattainable on Monday has become routine on Saturday.
rows.source: Indra Devi, Yoga for You: A Complete 6 Weeks' Course for Home Practice (Preston: A. Thomas & Co., first printing February 1960), Lesson One, First Week, 'What the Course Is and How to Use It'

rows.line: With morning yoga, Sting said, he had more energy, got more done, felt calmer.
rows.who: Sting, musician, UK
rows.quote: When I really do my Yoga in the morning, I have more energy in the day. I get more done. My mind is more composed.

flags.problem: Overclaim. The PubMed abstract says people of all ages (18 to 68) believed they had changed a lot but 'would change relatively little in the future', and calls this the 'end of history illusion'. The study shows people underestimate future change. It does not show that 'big changes' still lie ahead for everyone, and the measured change got smaller with age. The flat 'They are not' goes further than the source. The credit is correct.
flags.new_line: Young or old, we expect little change ahead. Researchers call this an illusion.

flags.problem: Wrong speaker in the credit. In the Siku Quanshu text (Wikisource juan 81, 道林養性第二), the passage opens '真人曰' (a 'Perfected One' says) before '養性之道，常欲小勞，但莫大疲及強所不能堪耳'. So the words come from an unnamed master quoted in Sun Simiao's book, not from Sun himself. The line is a faithful rendering and is fine as written.
flags.new_credit: Quoted by Sun Simiao · Qianjin Yaofang, c. 652

flags.problem: Kipchoge won Berlin 2015 in 2:04:00, a personal best. 'Had a bad race day' reads as if he raced badly. His own words were 'just had bad luck on the day' (Capital FM page confirmed).
flags.new_line: Even Kipchoge tested his shoes in Kenya, yet had bad luck on race day.

flags.problem: Added claim under Kuvalayananda's name: 'an Ashtanga drishti' is not in his text (archive.org p. 48 confirmed). 'Steadies' is also stronger than his words 'a perceptibly beneficial effect upon the unsteady mind'. His own term 'Nasagra-Drishti' keeps the link for Ashtanga readers.
flags.new_line: Nasagra drishti, the nose-tip gaze, kept up for months, helps steady a wandering mind.

flags.problem: Too general. LIFTMOR only studied postmenopausal women with low bone mass (osteopenia or osteoporosis, average age 65): 101 women, two supervised 30-minute sessions a week for 8 months. 'Older women' widens this to all older women. The trial was randomised and its title says 'Improves', so 'improved' is no stronger than the source.
flags.new_line: Two short, heavy lifting sessions a week improved weak bones in older women.

flags.problem: The line is fine (AH Sutrasthana 2.1: 'brahme muhurta uttishthet svastho rakshartham ayushah'). The credit 'Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutra 2.1' is confusing for this audience: Ashtanga students will read 'Sutra 2.1' as Patanjali's Yoga Sutra 2.1. The section is Sutrasthana.

Added claim under Iyengar's name: he never mentions 'Ashtanga'. His text (Light on Yoga p. 58, confirmed) says stiffness is conquered by regular practice and that morning practice makes one work better. The new line still lands slide 10 on daily practice, which the rule allows.
flags.new_line: Set the alarm: regular practice eases stiffness, and morning practice helps you work better.

judged.why: The study shows only that people of every age predict little future change, and it calls that an illusion. The flat 'They are not' says big changes lie ahead for everyone, which goes further than the source. The study also found that measured change gets smaller with age. The fix keeps the finding and the paper's own word 'illusion'. It is 13 words and the credit is correct.
judged.final_line: Young or old, we expect little change ahead. Researchers call this an illusion.

judged.why: I checked the Wikisource Siku Quanshu text (juan 81, 道林養性第二). The passage opens '眞人曰' right before '養性之道，常欲小勞，但莫大疲及強所不能堪耳'. So an unnamed 'Perfected One' says these words, and Sun Simiao quotes him. Putting the words straight under Sun's name names the wrong speaker. The line itself is a faithful rendering and stays as it is.
judged.final_line: The body needs a little work each day, never too tiring, never forced.
judged.final_credit: Quoted by Sun Simiao · Qianjin Yaofang, c. 652

judged.why: Kipchoge won Berlin 2015 in a personal best of 2:04:00, even with his insoles slipping. 'A bad race day' reads as if he raced badly or lost. His own words were 'just had bad luck on the day'. The fix uses his phrase, adds no claim and is exactly 14 words.
judged.final_line: Even Kipchoge tested his shoes in Kenya, yet had bad luck on race day.

judged.why: 'An Ashtanga drishti' is not in Kuvalayananda's text, so it adds a claim under his name. 'Steadies' is also stronger than his 'a perceptibly beneficial effect upon the unsteady mind'. His own term 'Nasagra-Drishti' still links to Ashtanga for this audience, and 'helps steady' matches his softer claim. The fix is 14 words.
judged.final_line: Nasagra drishti, the nose-tip gaze, kept up for months, helps steady a wandering mind.

judged.why: LIFTMOR studied only postmenopausal women with low bone mass (osteopenia or osteoporosis). 'Older women' stretches the finding to all older women. Adding 'weak bones' brings back the right group. The trial was randomised and its title says 'Improves', so 'improved' is no stronger than the source. The fix is 13 words.
judged.final_line: Two short, heavy lifting sessions a week improved weak bones in older women.

judged.why: The verse is Sutrasthana chapter 2, verse 1. 'Sutra 2.1' is a wrong form of the reference, and Ashtanga students will read it as Patanjali's Yoga Sutra 2.1, which is a different text. Only the credit needs fixing. The line matches 'brahme muhurte uttishthet svastho rakshartham ayushah'.
judged.final_line: Ayurveda's alarm clock: a healthy person rises before dawn, to protect a long life.

judged.why: In this passage Iyengar does not mention Ashtanga as a practice. Putting 'Ashtanga each morning' under his name adds a claim and merges his two separate points. His text says regular practice conquers stiffness and morning practice helps you work better. The fix keeps both points apart, is 14 words, and still lands slide 10 on daily practice.
judged.final_line: Set the alarm: regular practice eases stiffness, and morning practice helps you work better.
judged.final_credit: B. K. S. Iyengar · Light on Yoga, 1966

verified.quote: Without firm foundations a house cannot stand.
verified.original: 1. Without firm foundations a house cannot stand. Without the practice of the principles of yama and niyama, which lay down firm foundations for building character, there cannot be an integrated personality. Practice of asanas without the backing of yama and niyama is mere acrobatics.
verified.who: B. K. S. Iyengar, yoga teacher, Pune
verified.source: B. K. S. Iyengar, Light on Yoga (Yoga Dipika) (London: George Allen & Unwin, 1966), Part II, 'Hints and Cautions for the Practice of Asanas', The Requisites, no. 1, p. 57
verified.meaning: Like a house, practice needs firm foundations: good conduct and self-discipline.
verified.credit: B. K. S. Iyengar · Light on Yoga, 1966
verified.reason: Checked word for word in the OCR of the Allen & Unwin scan. The page header 'LIGHT ON YOGA 58' comes right after this item, so p. 57 is correct. The scan shows no print date. The first edition was 1966, and the page numbers match it. FIX: in the book, the 'foundation' is yama and niyama. A meaning line about the house alone drops what Iyengar meant, so the new line keeps his point in plain words. Different from the used Light on Yoga passages (headstand fear, effortless ease). Safe: a building metaphor with no disaster imagery. Frame it positively (build the foundation), not as collapse.

verified.quote: [Asanas] secure a fine physique, which is strong and elastic without being muscle bound... But their real importance lies in the way they train and discipline the mind.
verified.original: Asanas have been evolved over the centuries so as to exercise every muscle, nerve and gland in the body. They secure a fine physique, which is strong and elastic without being muscle bound and they keep the body free from disease. They reduce fatigue and soothe the nerves. But their real importance lies in the way they train and discipline the mind.
verified.who: B. K. S. Iyengar, yoga teacher, Pune
verified.source: B. K. S. Iyengar, Light on Yoga (London: George Allen & Unwin, 1966), Part I Introduction, section 'Asana', p. 42
verified.meaning: Asanas build a strong, supple body, but above all they train the mind.
verified.credit: B. K. S. Iyengar · Light on Yoga, 1966
verified.reason: Checked in the 1966 scan: the 'Asana' section of the Introduction, page header 'LIGHT ON YOGA 42'. The ellipsis correctly cuts 'and they keep the body free from disease. They reduce fatigue and soothe the nerves', so the slide makes no health or cure claim. FIX: on a slide, 'They' has nothing to refer to, so I replaced it with '[Asanas]'. I also changed the meaning line to keep Iyengar's emphasis that the mind matters most ('real importance'). Not on the used list. Safe.

verified.quote: What little bent is possible should first be secured and maintained for some time. After a while a bigger curve will become possible. In this way, with a daily practice, the spine will slowly be restored to its original state of elasticity.
verified.original: Halasana keeps the spinal column fully elastic. But people who find their spine stiffened, should start this exercise slowly. No jerks should be given. Jerks may injure the rigid muscles. What little bent is possible should first be secured and maintained for some time. After a while a bigger curve will become possible. In this way, with a daily practice, the spine will slowly be restored to its original state of elasticity.
verified.who: Swami Kuvalayananda, yoga teacher and researcher, founder of Kaivalyadhama, Lonavla
verified.source: Swami Kuvalayananda, Popular Yoga: Asanas, Part One (Lonavla: Kaivalyadhama; Bombay, 1933), ch. IV 'Cultural Poses', Halasana, 'Caution', pp. 80-81
verified.meaning: Start small; with daily practice a stiff spine slowly becomes flexible again.
verified.reason: Checked in the scan OCR. The title page reads 'Kaivalyadhama, Lonavla, Bombay-India 1933'. The page number '80' and the running head 'IV Cultural Poses' fall between 'should first be' and 'secured', so pp. 80-81 is correct. The only OCR fixes were 'secnred' and 'cnrve'. The text is gentle and focused on safety. The book's later note says the same caution applies to other back-bends. Not on the used list. Safe. Optional trim for a slide: the quote is 42 words.

verified.quote: The practice of Pranayama develops a steady mind, strong will-power and sound judgement.
verified.original: Pranayama is a conscious prolongation of inhalation, retention and exhalation... The practice of Pranayama develops a steady mind, strong will-power and sound judgement.
verified.who: B. K. S. Iyengar, yoga teacher, Pune
verified.source: B. K. S. Iyengar, Light on Pranayama (London: George Allen & Unwin, 1981), Part One, ch. 2 'Stages of Yoga', para. 16, p. 10
verified.meaning: Breathing practice builds a steady mind, strong will and good judgement.
verified.credit: B. K. S. Iyengar · Light on Pranayama, 1981
verified.reason: Checked in the file Light_on_Pranayama__B_K_S_Iyengar_djvu.txt in that archive.org item. The copyright page says 'First published in Great Britain by George Allen & Unwin 1981'. The sentence follows para. 16 under 'Pranayama' in ch. 2 'Stages of Yoga', and comes after the page header 'Light on Pranayama' for p. 10, so p. 10 is right. Light on Pranayama is not on the used list. Safe. The Preface passage 'Each morning I got up to practise...' is also confirmed in the same scan, if a daily-practice story is wanted.

verified.quote: ...the habit of deep, prolonged, rhythmic breathing, in due course, establishes a corresponding state of mental equipoise.
verified.original: Whatever the spiritual claims be, one thing nevertheless is true that the habit of deep, prolonged, rhythmic breathing, in due course, establishes a corresponding state of mental equipoise. And this saves much of the dynamic energy of the nerves wasted during physical or mental discord, excitement, and confusion.
verified.who: Shri Yogendra, founder of The Yoga Institute (India and America)
verified.source: Shri Yogendra, Hatha Yoga Simplified (Bombay: The Yoga Institute; first edition April 1931), ch. I 'Care of the Respiratory Apparatus', section 'Sedative Nervous Effects', p. 51 of the archive.org scan (a reprint from 1950 or later)
verified.meaning: Slow, deep, steady breathing, made a habit, brings a calm, balanced mind.
verified.reason: The wording is confirmed in the scan OCR ('thine' read as 'thing'). It is on p. 51, under the running head 'Care of the Respiratory Apparatus' in ch. I. The table of contents puts 'Sedative Nervous Effects' at p. 48. FIX TO THE DATE: the scan is not the 1940 edition. Its edition list stops at a 'Fifth Reprint, August 1940', but the text reports patients admitted in 1941 and on 5 December 1949, so it was printed in 1950 or later. I cannot confirm that this passage was in the 1931 first edition, so the slide credit has no year. Nearby pages give case histories of asthma patients. Use only the sentence above. Not on the used list. Safe.

verified.quote: As you practice the same postures day by day, you will find your muscles stretching, your body growing more responsive and better controlled, until what seemed unattainable on Monday has become routine on Saturday.
verified.original: Once having decided, repeat your chosen routine every day for a week, in order to give yourself a chance to assimilate it before going on to the next week's set of instructions. As you practice the same postures day by day, you will find your muscles stretching, your body growing more responsive and better controlled, until what seemed unattainable on Monday has become routine on Saturday. Then you will be ready to go on to the next week's lesson.
verified.who: Indra Devi, yoga teacher
verified.source: Indra Devi, Yoga for You: A Complete 6 Weeks' Course for Home Practice (Preston: A. Thomas & Co., first printing February 1960), Lesson One, First Week, 'What the Course Is and How to Use It'
verified.meaning: Do the same asanas daily; what seems impossible Monday becomes normal by Saturday.
verified.reason: Checked in the scan OCR. The imprint reads 'A. Thomas & Co., Preston' and 'First printing, February, 1960'. The passage is under 'Lesson One / First Week / What the Course Is and How to Use It'. The wording is exact. Indra Devi is not on the used list. Safe and hopeful. 'Postures' is her word, and the meaning line's 'asanas' is a fair simplification.

verified.quote: But the most important thing is to do them regularly, without skipping. If you happen not to have time for all of them, do just a few, perhaps even only one when you are in a great hurry—but never omit them entirely.
verified.original: But the most important thing is to do them regularly, without skipping. If you happen not to have time for all of them, do just a few, perhaps even only one when you are in a great hurry—but never omit them entirely. Once you begin to skip, you are likely to do so more and more often until you stop exercising altogether.
verified.who: Indra Devi, yoga teacher
verified.source: Indra Devi, Yoga for You: A Complete 6 Weeks' Course for Home Practice (Preston: A. Thomas & Co., 1960), Lesson One, First Week, 'What the Course Is and How to Use It'
verified.meaning: Practise every day; if you are busy, do just one asana, but never skip.
verified.reason: Checked in the 1960 scan. It is the same section as L9, a paragraph later, and the wording is exact. The long dash is in the original. On the slide, a line break can replace it. The meaning line has no dash. 'Them' means her exercises. If the slide needs it, write '[your exercises]'. Safe. If L9 is also used, both come from the same page, so use one per carousel.

verified.quote: The Nasal Gaze is a fine exercise for the wandering mind. Its practice if undertaken with zest and carried over a period of some months continuously, has a perceptibly beneficial effect upon the unsteady mind.
verified.original: Fixing one's eyes upon one's tip of the nose is called Nasagra-Drishti in Sanskrit. Nasagra means the tip of the nose and Drishti means gaze... The Nasal Gaze is a fine exercise for the wandering mind. Its practice if undertaken with zest and carried over a period of some months continuously, has a perceptibly beneficial effect upon the unsteady mind.
verified.who: Swami Kuvalayananda, yoga teacher and researcher, founder of Kaivalyadhama, Lonavla
verified.source: Swami Kuvalayananda, Popular Yoga: Asanas, Part One (Lonavla: Kaivalyadhama; Bombay, 1933), ch. III 'Meditative Poses', 'Nasagra-Drishti or the Nasal Gaze', p. 48
verified.meaning: Kept up for some months, gazing at the nose tip steadies a wandering mind.
verified.reason: The wording is confirmed in the 1933 scan. FIX 1: the page is 48, not 47. In this scan the page numbers sit at the foot of each page, '47' ends the previous chapter, and ch. III begins on the page numbered 48. FIX 2: the meaning line now keeps the 'some months' condition. In the book, the very next lines are a caution: develop the gaze 'very slowly and cautiously', because it 'directly works upon the brain through the optic nerves'. Do not present it as a quick fix. Do not say Kuvalayananda was writing about Ashtanga. Here he describes the gaze as a seated meditative technique. Not on the used list.

verified.quote: The stiffness of the body is conquered by regular practice and one is able to do the asanas well... Practice in the morning makes one work better in one's vocation.
verified.original: 6. The best time to practise is either early in the morning or late in the evening. In the morning asanas do not come easily as the body is stiff. The mind, however, is still fresh but its alertness and determination diminish as time goes by. The stiffness of the body is conquered by regular practice and one is able to do the asanas well. In the evening, the body moves more freely than in the mornings, and the asanas come better and with greater ease. Practice in the morning makes one work better in one's vocation. In the evening it removes the fatigue of the day's strain and makes one fresh and calm.
verified.who: B. K. S. Iyengar, yoga teacher, Pune
verified.source: B. K. S. Iyengar, Light on Yoga (London: George Allen & Unwin, 1966), Part II, 'Hints and Cautions for the Practice of Asanas', 'Time', no. 6, pp. 57-58
verified.meaning: Regular practice overcomes stiffness, and morning practice helps you do your work better.
verified.credit: B. K. S. Iyengar · Light on Yoga, 1966
verified.reason: Checked in the 1966 scan ('ananas' read as 'asanas'). The page break, marked by the header 'LIGHT ON YOGA 58', falls inside 'determina-/tion', so pp. 57-58 is correct. FIX: the old meaning line said 'morning practice loosens a stiff body'. Iyengar says the morning body is stiff, and that regular practice overcomes the stiffness. The new line keeps those two points apart. The ellipsis leaves out an evening sentence, which is fair. Different from the used Light on Yoga passages. Safe.

verified.quote: Every day is a good day.
verified.original: 日日是好日 (Japanese: nichinichi kore kōjitsu). Full case: 舉雲門垂語云：「十五日已前不問汝，十五日已後道將一句來。」自代云：「日日是好日。」
verified.who: Yunmen Wenyan (864-949), Chan (Zen) master, China
verified.source: Blue Cliff Record (Biyan lu), case 6 (碧巖錄第六則), compiled by Yuanwu Keqin, 1125; Chinese text on Wikisource 碧巖錄/卷第一; literal translation. Dictionary: Digital Daijisen and Koji Seigo o Shiru Jiten on Kotobank (日日是好日)
verified.meaning: Each new day, whatever it brings, can be a good day.
verified.reason: I checked the Chinese word for word on zh.wikisource (碧巖錄/卷第一, 第六則) and on the English Wikipedia page. Kotobank has Daijisen ('every day is a peaceful, good day') and Koji Seigo o Shiru Jiten ('a way of mind that values each day'), and both cite 碧巌録 case 6. I changed only the 'who' line. Yunmen lived 864-949 and taught mostly after the Tang fell, so 'late Tang' is not accurate. Giving his dates also avoids naming any ruling house. Blue Cliff case 16 was used before; case 6 was not. The line is safe and hopeful.

verified.quote: In truth it's all uncertain, but our desires want things to be certain. What can we do? We must be patient.
verified.original: English translation published by Wat Nong Pah Pong; Thai original not shown on the page.
verified.who: Ajahn Chah, Thai forest monk (Wat Nong Pah Pong)
verified.source: Ajahn Chah, '"Not Sure!" - The Standard of the Noble Ones', informal evening talk to monks and novices at his kuti (footnote 1 dates it 1980; footnote 8 dates 'this year' to 2522 BE = 1979 CE). In The Teachings of Ajahn Chah on ajahnchah.org (listed in the 'Food for the Heart' part), © Wat Nong Pah Pong 2007; translator not named
verified.meaning: Nothing in life is sure; we wish it were, so we practise patience.
verified.credit: Ajahn Chah · Not Sure!, Dhamma talk
verified.reason: I downloaded the page and found the exact wording. The next line is 'The most important thing is khanti, patient endurance', so the meaning line is faithful. The page shows a dating conflict (footnote 1 says 1980, footnote 8 says 1979), so the credit gives no year. Do not print a Thai keyword (ไม่แน่) unless it has been checked against a Thai edition. Not in used_who3. The tone is calm, not fearful. Avoid the nearby lines about defilements dying and 'expect only suffering'.

verified.quote: Going for a day? Take bread for a week.
verified.original: Едешь на день, бери хлеба на неделю.
verified.who: Russian proverb
verified.source: V. I. Dal, Poslovitsy russkogo naroda (Proverbs of the Russian People), 1862, section 'Запас' (Provision); literal translation
verified.meaning: Always pack more than you think you will need, before you leave.
verified.reason: I fetched the raw Wikisource text of Dal's section 'Запас'. Line 11 reads exactly 'Едешь на день, бери хлеба на неделю.' The variant 'Поезжай на неделю, а хлеба бери на две' and the backups 'Запасливый лучше богатого' and 'Хлеб в пути не тягость' are in the same section too. There is no water, weather or danger image. The Russian proverbs used before (slower you go, first pancake, eyes frighten, repetition, live and learn, stone and moss, old but sturdy) are all different.

verified.quote: Going into the forest? Don't forget your bush knife.
verified.original: เข้าเถื่อนอย่าลืมพร้า (khao thuean ya luem phra)
verified.who: Thai saying (สำนวน)
verified.source: Thai saying. The Royal Institute (ORST) dictionary uses it as the example under เถื่อน ('น. ป่า เช่น เข้าเถื่อนอย่าลืมพร้า'; seen in a reproduction at online-english-thai-dictionary.com, because the ORST site was down). Meaning from Thai PBS Podcast, นิทานสุภาษิต EP. 34 'เข้าเถื่อนอย่าลืมพร้า เข้าป่าอย่าลืมมีด': 'ให้มีความรอบคอบ อย่าประมาท' (be careful, not careless), like carrying a knife into the forest for when it is needed. Also Thai Wiktionary and Wongnai. Literal translation
verified.meaning: Before you set out, bring what you need. Be careful, not careless.
verified.credit: Thai saying · khao thuean ya luem phra
verified.reason: dictionary.orst.go.th returned 503 or reset the connection again. Other sources confirm the saying instead: a Royal Institute dictionary reproduction gives it as the usage example for เถื่อน (forest), Thai PBS (a public broadcaster) explains it, and Thai Wiktionary and Wongnai agree. I made two fixes. The RI dictionary glosses เถื่อน as plain 'forest', so I changed 'wild forest' to 'forest'. I also rewrote the meaning line to follow the Thai PBS gloss, which says to carry what you need, be careful and not careless. A พร้า is a farm and bush knife, so show it as a tool and never as a weapon. Re-check against ORST when the site is back up.

verified.quote: The way to nourish life: always do a little work, but never to great fatigue, and never force what you cannot bear.
verified.original: 養性之道，常欲小勞，但莫大疲及強所不能堪耳。
verified.who: A 'Perfected One' (真人, zhenren) quoted by the Tang physician Sun Simiao
verified.source: Sun Simiao, Beiji Qianjin Yaofang (Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold), c. 652, 'Nourishing Life' (養性), section 道林養性第二; juan 81 in the Siku Quanshu text on Wikisource (juan numbers differ between editions); literal translation
verified.meaning: Move your body a little every day, but never exhaust it or force it.
verified.reason: I fetched the Siku text of juan 81. Under the anchor 道林飬性第二 it reads '眞人曰…飬性之道常欲小勞但莫大疲及强所不能堪耳' (the Siku text uses the variant 飬 for 養). The translation is faithful. Quote only this sentence. The sentence before it is about long life and the one after is the 'flowing water' image. The sentence after that ('long sitting harms...') repeats the used Suwen ch. 23 item, so leave it out. Sun Simiao is not in used_who3.

verified.quote: Those of old who knew the Way... ate and drank in measure, kept regular hours, and did not wear themselves out recklessly; so body and spirit stayed together.
verified.original: 上古之人，其知道者，法於陰陽，和於術數，食飲有節，起居有常，不妄作勞，故能形與神俱
verified.who: Qi Bo, physician-teacher in the Suwen
verified.source: Suwen (Basic Questions), Chinese medical classic, ch. 1 'Shanggu tianzhen lun' (上古天真論); literal translation
verified.meaning: Eat well, rest on time, don't overdo it: body and mind stay together.
verified.reason: I checked the Chinese on Wikisource (素問第一卷, 上古天真論篇第一). It continues '而盡終其天年，度百歲乃去' (the legendary age of 100), which is left out. I made three fixes. First, the old meaning line had 15 words and added 'strong', which is not in the text; the new line has 13. Second, I put back the subject ('those of old who knew the Way') and marked the skipped clause with '...'. Third, the source line no longer names 'Huangdi Neijing', because that title names the Yellow Emperor, a legendary ruler and Qi Bo's questioner. This follows the credits used for Suwen ch. 2 and ch. 23. Chapter 1 was not used before.

verified.quote: The perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing: it refuses nothing. It receives, but does not keep.
verified.original: 至人之用心若鏡，不將不迎，應而不藏，故能勝物而不傷。
verified.who: Zhuangzi, Daoist sage
verified.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 7, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer (London: Bernard Quaritch, 1889)
verified.meaning: Let your mind be like a mirror: meet everything, cling to nothing.
verified.credit: Zhuangzi · ch. 7, tr. H. A. Giles, 1889
verified.reason: I downloaded the Gutenberg text. Chapter VII has 'For the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing: it refuses nothing. It receives, but does not keep.' The title page reads London, Bernard Quaritch, 1889, so this is a public-domain translation. The quote matches the text, with the opening 'For' dropped. Do not print Giles' chapter title 'How to Govern' (應帝王 refers to emperors and kings). Do not use the shaman story before the passage or the Hundun story after it. Zhuangzi ch. 7 is not in used_who3.

verified.quote: Joshu asked Nansen: "What is the path?" Nansen said: "Everyday life is the path."
verified.original: 南泉因趙州問。如何是道。泉云。平常心是道。(literally 'Ordinary mind is the Way'; Japanese 平常心 heijōshin)
verified.who: Nanquan (Nansen), Chan master, answering his student Zhaozhou (Joshu)
verified.source: Wumen Huikai, The Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), case 19 '平常是道', 1228, tr. Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 1934. Japanese dictionary sense of 平常心: Digital Daijisen on Kotobank
verified.meaning: The path is here, in your calm, ordinary, everyday mind.
verified.reason: The mirror page gives the Senzaki/Reps 1934 text exactly: case '19. Everyday Life Is the Path', with the quoted lines. I matched the Chinese on zh.wikisource 無門關 (十九 平常是道). Daijisen on Kotobank defines 平常心 as 'a mind no different from usual; a state of mind that does not waver', and Nihon Kokugo Daijiten names 無門関 as a source. So 'calm' in the meaning line fits the Japanese sense. Gateless Gate cases 7 and 28 and the 'road down the mountain' saying were used before; case 19 was not. It is safe.

verified.quote: In caring for the body and nourishing life, take care with small things. Do not skip a small gain as not worth doing, nor ignore a small harm as harmless. Gathering small things is how you reach the great.
verified.original: 故治身養性，務謹其細，不可以小益為不平而不修，不可以小損為無傷而不防。凡聚小所以就大，積一所以至億也。
verified.who: Ge Hong, Daoist writer (283-343)
verified.source: Ge Hong, Baopuzi Neipian (The Master Who Embraces Simplicity, Inner Chapters), ch. 13 'Jiyan' (極言); literal translation
verified.meaning: Small daily care for your body adds up to something big.
verified.reason: I fetched the raw text of 抱朴子 內篇·卷十三 極言 on Wikisource. The passage matches word for word. The translation is faithful; it drops only the second half of the last sentence (積一所以至億). The 'sown grain grows lush unnoticed' image just before it (益之者如苗禾之播殖…忽茂矣) is real and safe. The chapter opens on immortals, so credit only this line and make no claim about long life. The idea overlaps with used items by Hesiod, Xunzi and Ninomiya, but the source and wording are new. If the slide needs to be shorter, cut the middle sentence and mark the cut with '...'.

verified.quote: ...we may find it not so interesting to cook the same thing over and over again every day... If you lose the spirit of repetition it will become quite difficult, but it will not be difficult if you are full of strength and vitality.
verified.original: English original
verified.who: Shunryu Suzuki, Zen teacher
verified.source: Shunryu Suzuki, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind (1970), chapter 'Repetition', p. 55 (per the Shunryu Suzuki archive at cuke.com)
verified.meaning: Doing the same practice every day stays easy when you bring it energy.
verified.credit: Shunryu Suzuki · Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind
verified.reason: I downloaded the page. The exact wording is there, and the page says 'Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind - p.55'. The only cut is 'It is rather tedious, you may say.' The book is still in copyright, so keep the quote short; the chapter epigraph 'If you lose the spirit of repetition, your practice will become quite difficult' would also work. The chapter has two lines that must never be quoted or shown: 'we may laugh at it' about Indian ascetic practice, and 'If an artist becomes too idealistic, he will commit suicide'. The 'fog' and 'sitting' passages were used before; this one is clearly different.

verified.quote: Do not think karate is only in the dojo.
verified.original: 道場のみの空手と思ふな
verified.who: Gichin Funakoshi, founder of Shotokan karate
verified.source: Shōtōkan Nijū Kun (Twenty Precepts of Karate), no. 8, by Gichin Funakoshi. Said to have been written down around 1890; first published in Nakasone Genwa, Karate-dō Taikan (空手道大觀), 3 May 1938, frontispiece (per Japanese and English Wikipedia); literal translation
verified.meaning: Your training is not only for the dojo; it is for daily life.
verified.reason: Japanese Wikipedia (松濤館二十訓, and the 船越義珍 article, which cites Nakasone's 1938 frontispiece) gives the precept exactly as '道場のみの空手と思ふな'. English Wikipedia renders it 'Karate goes beyond the dojo.' The old meaning line had 15 words; the new one has 13 and stays with precept 8, while 'for all of life' belongs to precept 9. Use only this precept, never the full list: others mention enemies, battle and swords, and no. 11 is a water image. Funakoshi's memoir was used before; the precepts are a different source. He is a martial arts teacher, not a military figure, the same as the Musashi and Ueshiba items used before.

verified.quote: Who rises early, God gives to him.
verified.original: Кто рано встает, тому Бог подает.
verified.who: Russian proverb
verified.source: V. I. Dal, Poslovitsy russkogo naroda, 1862, section 'Работа — Праздность' (Work and Idleness); literal translation. Meaning from Russian Wiktionary: 'the earlier a person gets up, the more useful things they manage to do'
verified.meaning: Rise early, and you get more good things done.
verified.reason: I fetched Dal's section 'Работа — Праздность' from Wikisource. Line 273 reads exactly 'Кто рано встает, тому Бог подает.' 'Терпение и труд — все перетрут' is also there. I fixed the meaning line. The old line ('receive good gifts from God each day') was too literal and missed the sense in Wiktionary: the earlier you rise, the more useful work you get done. God is mentioned respectfully. The link to early Mysore practice is AYBKK's own and should not be presented as the proverb's meaning. Not in used_who3.

verified.quote: [The days] come and go like muffled and veiled figures, sent from a distant friendly party; but they say nothing; and if we do not use the gifts they bring, they carry them as silently away.
verified.original: Same (written in English, 1870). Emerson's text begins "They come and go..."; "[The days]" replaces "They".
verified.who: Ralph Waldo Emerson, American essayist (1803-1882)
verified.source: "Works and Days", in Society and Solitude: Twelve Chapters (Boston: Fields, Osgood & Co., 1870), essay begins p. 139; Project Gutenberg eBook #69258
verified.meaning: Each new day comes hidden but friendly, with gifts; use them before they go.
